landing.heroLead: Model, version, and navigate your architecture with the C4 model. The model is the source of truth — diagrams are only projections.
landing.featuresSectionLead: Every architectural decision is traceable, every version is immutable, every relationship is a first-class entity.
landing.cta2Lead: Create your first workspace, model your system, and make your first commit in minutes.
landing.feature1Desc: Move across Context, Container, Component and Code with native hierarchy.
landing.feature2Desc: Every commit is a full snapshot. Traceable history and branching.
landing.feature3Desc: Elements and relationships are first-class entities, not just drawings.
landing.feature4Desc: Multi-team workspaces with scoped access control.
landing.feature5Desc: Edit freely, commit when ready. No loss of context.
landing.feature6Desc: Full JSON for portability. CI/CD pipeline integration.

redis.description: In-memory key-value store used as a cache, session store or message broker.

kafka.description: Distributed event-streaming platform for high-throughput durable topics.

flow-divider.label: Named line

deploy-sharded-store.label: Sharded store

deploy-shard.label: Shard

deploy-shard-router.label: Shard router
deploy-shard-router.description: The router in front of a store's shards (mongos, vtgate).

k8s-cluster.label: Kubernetes cluster
k8s-cluster.description: A Kubernetes cluster with its distribution, version, nodes and zones; holds namespaces and workloads.

k8s-namespace.label: Namespace
k8s-namespace.description: A Kubernetes namespace inside a cluster, optionally with mesh sidecar injection.

k8s-workload.label: Workload
k8s-workload.description: A Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob or Pod, with replicas, autoscaling, image and resources.

k8s-service.label: Service
k8s-service.description: A Kubernetes Service in front of a workload: its type and port.

k8s-ingress.label: Ingress
k8s-ingress.description: A Kubernetes Ingress: the host and class traffic enters the cluster by.

k8s-container.label: Container
k8s-container.description: A container of a workload's pod: the main one, a sidecar (proxy, logs, secrets, metrics) or an init container run first, in order.

shared-ref.label: Reference
shared-ref.description: A reference to a shared element, drawn near its consumers; edges to it are edges to the element.

userTemplates.emptyHint: Select nodes on the canvas and click 'Save as template'

publisher-subscriber.name: Publisher-Subscriber
publisher-subscriber.description: A publisher sends each event once to a topic and every subscriber gets its own copy. Use it to add consumers without touching the producer; the trade-off is eventual consistency and harder end-to-end tracing.

fan-out.name: Fan-out (topic → queues)
fan-out.description: A topic delivers each message to one queue per consumer, so every consumer reads at its own pace, retries independently and can fail without affecting the others. Costs one queue per consumer to operate.

queue-based-load-leveling.name: Queue-Based Load Leveling
queue-based-load-leveling.description: A queue absorbs bursts between the callers and a service that can only work at a steady rate, protecting it and its database. Responses become asynchronous and the queue can build a backlog.

competing-consumers.name: Competing Consumers
competing-consumers.description: Several identical workers read from the same queue; each message is handled by exactly one of them. Scales throughput horizontally; ordering across messages is lost and handlers must be idempotent.

async-request-reply.name: Asynchronous Request-Reply
async-request-reply.description: The API accepts a long-running request with 202 Accepted and a status URL, hands the work to a queue, and the client polls until a worker records the result. Keeps the API responsive at the cost of polling and a status store.

claim-check.name: Claim Check
claim-check.description: A large payload is stored in object storage and only a reference travels through the broker; the receiver fetches the payload with it. Keeps messages small and cheap; adds a storage round trip and payload lifecycle to manage.

pipes-and-filters.name: Pipes and Filters
pipes-and-filters.description: Processing is split into independent stages connected in sequence, each doing one transformation. Stages scale and deploy separately; the whole pipeline adds latency and needs per-stage error handling.

scatter-gather.name: Scatter-Gather
scatter-gather.description: An aggregator sends the same request to several services in parallel and combines their replies into one answer, with a timeout for slow responders. Good for quotes and searches; the slowest reply bounds latency.

api-gateway.name: API Gateway (Gateway Routing)
api-gateway.description: One entry point routes each request to the right service by path or host and handles cross-cutting concerns (auth, TLS, rate limits). Clients see one API; the gateway becomes a critical component to scale and keep thin.

backends-for-frontends.name: Backends for Frontends (BFF)
backends-for-frontends.description: Each kind of client gets its own backend shaped for its screens and calls, in front of shared services. Frontends evolve independently; some logic is duplicated across BFFs.

gateway-aggregation.name: Gateway Aggregation
gateway-aggregation.description: The gateway turns one client request into several backend calls and returns a single combined response, saving round trips on slow networks. The gateway takes on composition logic and the slowest call's latency.

static-content-hosting.name: Static Content Hosting
static-content-hosting.description: Static assets are served from object storage through a CDN, so the application only handles dynamic requests. Cheaper and faster at the edge; deploys must invalidate cached content.

load-balancer-reverse-proxy.name: Load Balancer / Reverse Proxy
load-balancer-reverse-proxy.description: A load balancer spreads requests across identical instances and takes unhealthy ones out of rotation. Gives horizontal scale and availability; instances should be stateless or share state elsewhere.

cqrs.name: CQRS
cqrs.description: Commands and queries use separate models and stores: writes go to a normalized store, and change events build a read model shaped for queries. Each side scales and evolves on its own; reads are eventually consistent.

event-sourcing.name: Event Sourcing
event-sourcing.description: State is stored as an append-only log of events; projections replay the log into read models. You get a full audit trail and can rebuild views; queries need projections and event schemas must evolve carefully.

transactional-outbox.name: Transactional Outbox
transactional-outbox.description: The service writes its data and the event to publish in one local transaction (an outbox table); a relay or CDC process then publishes the outbox to the broker. Avoids dual writes; delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.

saga-orchestration.name: Saga — Orchestration
saga-orchestration.description: An orchestrator runs a business transaction as a sequence of local steps and, when one fails, sends compensating commands to undo the steps already done. The flow is explicit and observable; the orchestrator must be durable and stay free of business rules that belong to the services.

saga-choreography.name: Saga — Choreography
saga-choreography.description: There is no coordinator: each service reacts to the previous step's event and emits its own, compensating on failure events. Services stay decoupled; the overall flow is implicit and harder to follow and test.

cache-aside.name: Cache-Aside
cache-aside.description: The application reads from the cache first; on a miss it reads the database and populates the cache. Simple and resilient to cache loss; data can be stale until expiry or explicit invalidation.

cache-write-through-behind.name: Write-Through / Write-Behind Cache
cache-write-through-behind.description: Writes go to the cache, which persists them to the database synchronously (write-through) or asynchronously in batches (write-behind). Reads are always warm; write-behind risks losing writes if the cache fails.

materialized-view.name: Materialized View
materialized-view.description: A builder listens to changes in the source stores and keeps a precomputed view shaped for one query. Expensive joins become a single read; the view lags behind its sources.

data-replication.name: Data Replication (Primary-Replica)
data-replication.description: Writes go to the primary, which replicates to read replicas that take the read traffic. Scales reads and adds failover candidates; asynchronous replicas can serve stale data.

sharding.name: Sharding
sharding.description: Data is split across shards by a partition key and a router sends each request to the shard that owns its key. Scales writes and storage beyond one node; cross-shard queries and rebalancing get hard.

bulkhead.name: Bulkhead
bulkhead.description: Workloads are split into isolated pools (workers, connections, threads) by criticality or tenant, so one overloaded or failing pool cannot drain the others. Contains failures; each pool is sized separately and can sit idle.

multi-region-active-passive.name: Multi-region — Active-Passive (DR)
multi-region-active-passive.description: One region serves traffic while a standby region receives replicated data and takes over on failover. Backup & restore, pilot light and warm standby are this shape with less running in the standby; recovery time grows as the standby shrinks.

multi-region-active-active.name: Multi-region — Active-Active
multi-region-active-active.description: Every region serves traffic and data is replicated between them, so users hit the nearest healthy region (the Geode pattern). Lowest latency and recovery time; writes need conflict handling across regions.
